Transcript:
[00:00:05] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Avery from Redwood, AE on accounts in finance. With me is Diego, our SE who runs Optimize walkthroughs. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:15] Priya: Good thanks, Priya here. We're trying to nail down cost for our assistant and also keep p99 latency under 300ms for simple queries.
[00:00:25] Diego: Great, that's helpful. Just to set expectations, we'll show live config options: batching windows, KV cache & prefix cache strategies, and a simple cost model. We often see customers trade a bit of latency for 30-50% token cost savings.
[00:00:40] Carlos: Quick Q — our load is spiky, lots of short sessions, median seq length ~80 tokens but tail to 1k. 
[00:00:50] Diego: That's actually common. For short sessions prefix/KV caching gives outsized benefits. We'll show why.

[00:01:10] Diego: (shares screen) First slide — batching basics. Two knobs: batch window (ms) and max batch size. If you increase window to 25-50ms you get better throughput but add latency. For NovaFinance with p99 300ms target, we recommend 15-25ms window and adaptive batching that scales with request rate.
[00:01:35] Priya: Does Redwood's adaptive batching auto-shrink on tail latencies?
[00:01:40] Diego: Yeah — we have workload-aware windows: when you see spikes we prioritize latency SLOs and reduce batch window. There's an injectable policy you can tune per deployment.

[00:02:05] Avery: Now caching. Two patterns: prefix cache (response-level reuse for identical prefixes) and KV cache (token-level key-value cache for stateful convs). Prefix cache is great when you have many repeated system prompts or templates; KV is better for long-running dialogs where earlier KV can be re-used across steps.
[00:02:30] Carlos: For our flows we have a lot of near-duplicate prompts (same sys prompt + masked user fields). Sounds like prefix cache fits.
[00:02:40] Diego: Yes. Quick note on hit rate math: if you achieve 60-70% prefix hit rate on short queries, you can reduce generated token volume significantly — since hits avoid re-generating many tokens.

[00:03:10] Diego: (types) Here's a simple cost model. Baseline hosted generation cost = X tokens generated. With batching you lower per-token compute overhead ~10-20% depending on GPU kernel efficiency. Combine with prefix hits and KV hits and you multiply savings. Example we ran for a payments customer: 40% cost reduction from caching + 15% from batching = ~50% total.
[00:03:35] Priya: Can you show assumptions? Our prompts are variable length; sometimes user adds context.
[00:03:45] Diego: Sure — assumptions: avg request = 120 input tokens, avg generation = 60 tokens, 65% prefix hit, KV hit 10% (for long convs), batching efficiency 1.15x. Those map to savings in the attached spreadsheet. We'll share.

[00:04:20] Priya: What's the impact on p99 latency when prefix caching returns a cached response?
[00:04:25] Diego: Cache hits are usually sub-50ms local lookup + small routing, so p99 for hit traffic is often much lower than cold generation. Cold misses still go through normal runtime.
[00:04:40] Maya: Any concerns about correctness/regeneration when cached prompts depend on external state?
[00:04:45] Diego: Good callout. You need deterministic templates and clear cache keys. Redwood supports TTLs and tag-based invalidation; we recommend a short TTL for prompts that include ephemeral state and stronger validation if the template changes.

[00:05:10] Avery: Security & compliance quick note — for Private/Dedicated deployments we can integrate with your KMS and enforce customer-managed keys. Audit logs for cache access can be exported to your SIEM.
[00:05:25] Carlos: We need SOC2 + network diagram for on-prem option.
[00:05:30] Avery: We'll attach SOC2 report and a sample VPC deployment diagram in the follow-up.

[00:06:00] Diego: Back to cost model — i'll show a simulated run with NovaFinance-like traffic. (screen) Here: baseline tokens/day 1M, avg gen tokens 0.06M, with 65% prefix hit it reduces effective generated tokens to 0.35M. If hosted per-token unit is assumed, that's roughly 45% cost reduction before batching. With batching and quantization profile you get to ~55%.
[00:06:30] Priya: You said quantization helps too — will that change accuracy?
[00:06:35] Diego: We recommend mixed quantization profiles. For top-level intents we use 8-bit quant with calibrated FP fallback; accuracy impact is negligible for most tasks but we can run evals on your prompts.

[00:07:10] Priya: How invasive is the KV prefix integration? Our stack is Kubernetes with a custom session-store.
[00:07:15] Diego: Redwood exposes routing hooks and a small SDK to compute cache keys. KV cache can be either co-located (fast) or remote with Redis-like layer. For Kubernetes you'd deploy a lightweight cache process. We also support our managed cache in Dedicated mode.
[00:07:35] Carlos: If we use Dedicated GPUs, what's the delta in cost vs hosted?
[00:07:40] Avery: Depends on commit level. Typical finance customers see lower per-token compute with Dedicated at commit > $XXk/month. We'll send a modeled comparison for NovaFinance.

[00:08:05] Diego: Walkthrough of sample spreadsheet. Column A: request count; B: avg input tokens; C: avg gen tokens; D: prefix hit%; E: KV hit%; F: batching factor; G: effective generated tokens; H: cost estimate.
[00:08:25] Priya: Could you run one live with our sample numbers?
[00:08:30] Diego: We can if you share a 7-day sample. If not, i can demo with a proxied 'finance-like' profile.

[00:09:00] (Diego runs quick simulation with sample profile)
[00:10:00] Diego: Result: with prefix hit 63% and batching factor 1.12 we estimate 42% reduction in billable tokens compared to baseline. p50 latency increased ~10ms due to batching on average, but p99 stayed within your 300ms target in the simulated load.
[00:10:20] Priya: That's promising. What about cold-starts during burst — do you have warm pools?
[00:10:25] Diego: Yes, we support warm pools and predictive scaling. For short spikes we recommend a small warm buffer at peak hour windows plus autoscaling rules.

[00:11:00] Maya: Any operational caveats we should know? E.g., consistency of cache across AZs.
[00:11:05] Diego: For cross-AZ you can use regional caches with eventual consistency. For strict consistency stick to single AZ or synchronous replication — that adds latency. Most customers accept eventual consistency for cache entries that are re-usable.

[00:12:00] Carlos: If we wanted to invalidate cache when underlying template changes, how granular is invalidation?
[00:12:05] Diego: You can tag keys by template version and perform tag-based purge. TTLs also help. We'll provide example code.

[00:13:00] (brief pause)
[00:13:15] Priya: Questions on evaluation — we want to run quality regression tests if quantization or caching changes outputs.
[00:13:20] Avery: Redwood Optimize includes eval hooks that compare model outputs against your golden set. We can configure alerts for regressions beyond thresholds.
[00:13:35] Priya: Great. Can you include that in the pilot scope?
[00:13:40] Avery: Yes. We'll include evaluation and rollback plan.

[00:14:10] Diego: One more thing — cold cache traffic still consumes full tokens; the benefits grow over time as cache warms for repeated prompts. For transactional flows with many repeated templates you'll see fast wins.
[00:14:30] Carlos: Do you support partial generation caching (e.g., reuse KV cache up to certain layers)?
[00:14:35] Diego: You can cache intermediate KV states and rehydrate partially; it's a bit more complex but supported. We'll share config examples.

[00:15:00] (middle of call - skipping to end of detailed walkthrough)
[00:33:40] Diego: ...and the spreadsheet includes sensitivity analysis: hit-rate +-10% and batching factor +-0.1 show cost delta of ~8-12% in either direction. 
[00:34:05] Priya: That helps. If we provide real traffic we'll get exact numbers.
[00:34:10] Avery: Recap — we'll send pricing + pilot config, Diego will run the sim with your numbers, and we'll schedule the benchmark.
[00:34:20] Maya: One more item — legal wants encryption at rest details for cache and key management.
[00:34:25] Avery: Copy that. We'll include KMS architecture diagram and SOC2.
